How to read the turnings, and where they come from

Two American authors, William Strauss and Neil Howe, proposed that American history moves in cycles of about 80 to 85 years. Each cycle has four "turnings" of about 21 years, and people born in the same stretch form a "generation" with one of four archetypes. The idea is in their books Generations (1991) and The Fourth Turning (1997).
High. Institutions are strong and individualism is weak.
Awakening. Institutions are attacked and individualism rises.
Unraveling. Institutions are weak and distrusted, and individualism is strong.
Crisis. Institutions are rebuilt and individualism declines.
Prophet. Born in a High, comes of age in an Awakening.
Nomad. Born in an Awakening, comes of age in an Unraveling.
Hero. Born in an Unraveling, comes of age in a Crisis.
Artist. Born in a Crisis, comes of age in a High.

What it is not. It is a theory, not a record and not a measurement. Many historians do not accept it as science. Critics say it is too vague to be proven wrong, and that it fits a pattern onto events after the fact. It was built on American history from 1584, with an Anglo-American focus. The authors say similar cycles show up in other developed countries; I have not checked that, and it may not fit histories outside the West. The turning dates and the generation names on these pages are theirs. They say nothing about any one person in the family, and nothing on this page claims a person had a trait because of the year they were born.
Why it is here. Grouping the years helps me see a life next to its time. The names are theirs, and I like them.
Read more: the books, at Open Library (the primary source) · Strauss–Howe generational theory, on Wikipedia, which also lists the criticism with its sources.

An eight-digit serial beginning with 3 was used for men who entered through Selective Service, and the second digit 4 for the southeastern service area that included Alabama; so he probably entered by the draft. The 1943 Post says he "entered the service Sept. 27, 1942." Research file section 1 (serial-number references cited there) Plausible

The Cardiff marker (2010), as recorded on HMDB, names "JOBO" Country as "a WWII soldier with the Thunderbolt Division," which it says freed the Buchenwald camp and fought at the Battle of the Bulge. "Thunderbolt" is a nickname more than one division has used; the 83rd Infantry Division adopted it in early 1945. His own unit, regiment and company are not identified: no service record is in hand. The obituary's "Middle Eastern Service Medal with 1 Silver Star" is probably the European-African-Middle Eastern Campaign Medal with a silver service star, which Army guidance says is worn in place of five bronze stars. The 83rd is credited with five campaigns. A strong fit, not yet checked against his discharge. Research file section 2 (Army HRC guidance cited there) Plausible

William told the Southern Claims Commissioners that a colonel, or a man they called colonel, wanted him to go with the soldiers and show them the way, and that he did, about seven miles. His petition says the general "ordered" him from his home to go as pilot. The claim was rejected, but the testimony is his own, sworn in 1871 and 1872. The dates of the raid are as printed in the Wikipedia article on Wilson's Raid. The Official Records, Wilson's own report, are the primary source and have not been pulled yet.

2. The Graham place, Mount Olive township
Wilson's cavalry camped "at or near William Graham's on the public road leading from Jasper in Walker County to Elyton." Thomas James's claim 7105, quoted on William's sheet Documented
Wilson's troops took Nancy's mare, mule, corn, bacon and fodder "on or about" 28 March 1865. William was present. Claim 7100 p22 Documented

When the soldiers first came to the house, William says, "a Colonel, or at least they called him Colonel," told him he wanted him to go with them and pilot them, "which I did along 7 miles." While he was away his horses, bacon, fodder, saddle and the rest of the corn were taken. On his way home he saw his roan horse in the soldiers' hands. Present when the property was taken, he says: Penelopa Graham, his wife Rebecca, and his daughter Amanda (names as read from the image). Claim 7099, William's testimony, images 00455 to 00457 (my reading of the handwriting; the machine transcript says "guide") Documented

The petition says the same: the general in command, "whom petitioner supposed to be Genl Wilson, ordered petitioner from his home to go as pilot for said command seven miles," and he did. Claim 7099, petition, image 00437 Documented

Rebecca's testimony, badly faded, says the soldiers had carried him away as a guide, toward Elyton. Several words are lost. Claim 7099, Rebecca's testimony, images 00474 to 00475, as read in the transcript; not yet checked against the image Plausible

William says the army was said to have been held four or five days by high water at the Black Warrior River. He did not see this himself; it is hearsay in his testimony. Claim 7099, answer 14, image 00457 Documented

Did the army camp near the house? William says no: "No part of the army camped near my house." Thomas James's claim (7105) says the cavalry camped "at or near William Graham's." Both are sworn. They disagree. Claim 7099 image 00457; claim 7105 Unresolved

The date of the taking. Nancy's claim: on or about 28 March 1865. William's petition: about the last days of March. William's testimony: the corn was taken "about the end of April," which the transcript flags as probably a slip. Priscilla's petition: on or about 30 March and 1 April. Penelope's testimony reads March 25 (faint). The raid reached Elyton on 28 March. Claims 7100, 7099 (images 00436 and 00455) and 9849 Unresolved
The mark on the map is approximate: the middle of Thomas's land in Township 15 South, Range 3 West. William's own land is not placed on this map. Computed Plausible
3. Where William turned back, about seven miles toward Elyton

Placed seven miles along the straight line from the Graham place toward Elyton. Approximate: the record gives the distance and the direction, not the spot, and a road is longer than a straight line. Claim 7099, images 00437 and 00456 to 00457 (distance); Rebecca's testimony, image 00474 to 00475 (direction, "toward Elyton")

About seven miles from home William turned back. He says he "piloted" the command that far, then went home and found the property gone. The place is not named in any record. Claim 7099, images 00437 and 00456 to 00457 Documented
The distance is his and so is the direction, toward Elyton. The point on the map is only a mark seven miles along a straight line, not a place the records name. Computed Plausible

The soldiers he saw fed their horses about three miles from his house toward Elyton, he says, "or at least I saw signs of feeding." The figure is faint in the image. Claim 7099, answer 9, image 00456 Documented

What his neighbor said about him 1

Julian Nail, who lived within a mile and says he hid in the woods as a Union soldier, says William fed him there, and that William would go to Elyton, "about 18 miles away," learn what the rebel army was doing, and bring the news to him in the woods. Nail also says the boys with him said the rebels had threatened to burn William's place and hang him. Claim 7099, Julian Nail, images 00453 and 00454, as read in the machine transcript (not yet checked against the image) Documented

Where the army camped. William says not near his house. Thomas James's claim (7105) says the cavalry camped "at or near William Graham's." Both are sworn. Claim 7099 image 00457; claim 7105 Unresolved

When it happened. Nancy's claim: on or about 28 Mar 1865. William's petition: the last days of March. William's testimony: the corn was taken "about the end of April." Priscilla's petition: on or about 30 Mar and 1 Apr. Penelope: 25 March, faint. The raid reached Elyton on 28 Mar. Claims 7100, 7099 (images 00436 and 00455) and 9849, and Wikipedia, Wilson's Raid Unresolved

Who Penelope Graham is. Priscilla's sheet takes her as William's daughter-in-law, aged 26. In William's answer she is named apart from his wife and his daughter. We do not know whose wife she was. This is a gap to fill later. Claim 7099 images 00456 and 00477; claim 9849 Unresolved

Most southern family history was made on a small plot of ground where a person was born, lived, and died, and the old homeplace became precious and personal. One can clearly see in the mind's eye the old homeplace and revisit it in memory, years after the physical disappearance of the house through time, neglect, or progress. We must all go home again in reality or memory to reaffirm who we really are; retracing treasured memories of childhood is an unerasable part of one's identity; longing to walk again in the places of childhood and have a blessed sense of belonging.

When one becomes old enough to begin looking back with an appreciation for the places and culture that shaped and nurtured him, he begins to develop a keen sense of regret because of the wasted years of apathy and indifference toward the parents who dearly loved all their sons and daughters. As our country became more industrialized, later generations dreamed of far-away places, a better economic life, and left the lonely isolation of farm life to answer the call of the bright lights of the city.

Genealogy is devoid of the interesting human details about how our ancestors lived and died. Each generation must take nourishment from the past generation and give knowledge to the next one. Hopefully, this genealogy will make fascinating reading for thousands of descendants and will be kept and cherished by many future generations. It is a tribute to the noble characteristics of intelligence and integrity, and will help us recognize the human traits of the warm, unselfish, hospitable, and kind people who inhabited the area of North Alabama.

Life was difficult for many of those early families, especially for the farmers who could not read or write and who became indebted to the local merchant and sometimes lost their mortgaged farms in the battle of merchant versus farmer. Moving to another state was sometimes a rebellion against unbearably heavy and grossly unjust taxation. It was a life in which love, determination, and ingenuity usually prevailed.

p. 6Most of the early, rugged pioneers of Alabama were Scotch, Irish, Scotch-Irish, or English. Some folk tales and family legends about these people show they were clannish, thrifty, hardworking, hardheaded, stubborn, but were dependable, loyal, and men of their word. They drove a hard bargain but were tenderhearted and dearly loved their families. The southern states were settled by these types of people and retain these characteristics to this date, largely because relatives, friends, and neighbors settled in one section and gave a dominant tinge to creed, church, and customs, which grew stronger as sons and daughters of these families married.

For the newcomers, a variety of fruits, berries, and nuts were available for those who would harvest them, making the task of feeding a family easier. Mulberries, persimmons, plums, cherries, wild blueberries, wild blackberries, wild grapes, muscadines, hickory nuts, chestnuts, walnuts, and scaly bark grew in abundance. Meat was plentiful, furnished by rabbits, turkeys, partridges, wild ducks, wild geese, pheasants, and deer. Panthers, wild boars, and wild cats roamed the mountains surrounding the cleared farm land. Rivers, creeks, and streams teemed with fish in clear, clean, unpolluted waters.

Contrary to what is portrayed by various news media about the wealthy, leisure life in the pre-civil-war South, most families did not have slaves and worked like a slave themselves in the fields to barely survive. This was partly due to not believing in slavery and partly because not enough money was accumulated to buy a slave, which was very expensive.

In studying the history of the Virginia Colony, everyone was connected in one way or another with the development, either as financial backers or as settlers. The early Virginia settlers were out of London dealing in the tobacco trade, a profitable business venture. They secured their importance by being better educated and financially better off than the average person. Society in Virginia was never by class, as every white man, once out of the condition of indentured servant, was free to do as he pleased, and was the equal of other white men. Social distinction did exist but was never recognized by law.

Only the landowners could hold office; every man was a ruler on his own plantation and there were no feudal laws. Many immigrants came as poor men but joined the ranks of the wealthy by good management and hard work. In many instances, poor immigrants married widows and thereby gained control of their estates which gave a better start in becoming large landholders.

The position of the father in the family was a controlling factor in the movement of the children. Fathers usually willed the lands to favorite sons, which made it necessary for the others to migrate to a new region where land was plentiful and less costly. While the sons might have desired to leave sooner, departure was postponed by affection or necessity, since, in most cases, it was only after the probation of the will and disposal of the estate that enough money was available for traveling to the West or the South and acquiring cheaper lands. They plunged ahead, risking everything in a true pioneer spirit.

p. 7The Revolutionary War left its devastating effect on the personal life as well as the economic life of the early pioneers, which accounts for a large migration, during the 1785-1790 period of time, out of Virginia to the Carolinas and Georgia. In many cases, whole families moved with the sons, daughters, in-laws, grandchildren; suffering hardships and dangers that were indigenous to the raw regions. In many cases, the Revolutionary War Soldiers of VA served in the battles of South Carolina and after the war moved to that area following the Commanding Officer of their Virginia Militia.

The church was the center of community social and religious life which played an important role in family life of all generations. It acted as an anchor to help families endure the hardship and sadness of illness and early deaths at a time when medical care was not available in many areas. One can imagine the sadness of saying a tearful goodbye to parents, brothers, and sisters, knowing that the possibility of seeing them again was very remote. This happened in every generation when the children of the early settlers of Alabama married and moved with in-laws over into Mississippi for a few years and then on into Ark, Okla, Missouri, and Texas.

In Alabama many unique customs were practiced. After the crops were "laid by" in July, usually someone would hold a singing class for all the children to attend at the local church. Annual protracted revivals were held at night, usually by a guest preacher, and the people would come from miles around in their wagons with the children sitting in the back of the wagon with their legs swinging free.

May is the month for Decoration Day, one of those cultural relics which is a memorial to family members deceased and is still practiced in the rural areas. A few days before the decoration date, usually on Saturday, family members gather and clean grass and debris off the graves of loved ones. On Sunday, families of friends and relatives cluster at the graves, greeting each other with smiles, hugs, kisses, hand shakes, and pats on the back. They decorate the graves of white sand or grassy plots with wreaths, sprays, or bouquets of live or artificial flowers. Before the days of artificial flowers, live flowers gathered from the homeplace were placed in vases filled with water.

Also colored crepe paper was used to create attractive, handmade, life-like flowers. This craft is no longer practiced. After a memorial service in the church, everyone spreads the food on cloths on the ground (thus the expression of "dinner on the ground"), and later they gather inside the church for an afternoon of Gospel singing.

Another custom still practiced is gathering at a church during the summer months and have "all day singing." Sacred Harp singing is being revived, which is singing the notes rather than words, sometimes called "fa-so-la singing." It was said, "All day singing, dinner on the ground, liquor in the bushes, and the devil all around."

p. 8Very little cash was available to buy from a store so most necessities were made at home; socks were knit by hand, and most all of women's clothing was made at home. Leftover scraps of cloth from the making of dresses were used to make hand-made, attractive quilts out of necessity to keep warm in the winter when the houses were not insulated or heated as today. The art of quilting is being revived across the United States, with Quilting Clubs giving awards for the most original and attractive quilts. Scattered cotton gathered from the fields in the fall of the year was used as a filler for the quilts.

"Cotton Cards" were used to remove the seeds, burrs, and leaves, leaving it clean and fluffy. This was a wintertime chore. In one room, a quilting frame was suspended by cords from four hooks in the ceiling. When quilting the frame was let down to a comfortable level to quilt by hand. When not in use the cords were wound around the frame ends and it was left hanging near the ceiling, out of the way.

Fall of the year was molasses-making time. Each farmer gathered his cane by cutting the stalk, stripping the leaves, and hauling it in a wagon to the mill where the juice was pressed out into the first pan for cooking. At a certain stage of cooking, it was run off into a second pan, a third pan, and so on. When it was cooked to the right consistency, it was poured into buckets, jars, or whatever container made available by the farmer. Homemade molasses, rich in iron, was used in baking cookies and cakes or mixing with butter for a spread on hot biscuits on a cold winter morning. The expression "slow as molasses" developed because molasses would not pour when left stored in a cold kitchen.
On a winter day, it had to be spooned out of the container.

Making kraut was another task peformed [sic] during the crop "lay by" time, using the cabbages planted in early spring. After shredding the cabbage head, it was packed with salt in a crock vessel, usually a churn, allowed to ferment for a month or so then sealed in glass jars for the winter.

Before the age of super markets, most all food was grown and preserved on the farm for the long, winter months. Fruits and vegetables were canned in glass jars with metal lids or were dried on a sheet on a roof after being sliced thin, especially true of apples and peaches. Irish potatoes, sweet potatoes, and turnips were harvested in the fall and stored in cellars. If a cellar was not available, the harvest was piled on the ground and covered with soil to prevent freezing and removed as needed from an opening in the dirt mound.

Another unpopular, arm-aching chore was the daily or weekly churning of clabbered milk. Milk (rich with cream) was poured into a churn and set aside so that the milk could "turn" or clabber. The churn was tilted to its side to test the readiness of the milk for churning. If the milk held together in a solid form and separated cleanly from the side of the churn then the milk needed to be churned without delay. The churning process (agitating the clabbered milk) was done by using a dasher which was usually homemade. The dasher was a stick similar to a broom handle with one end nailed to the center of a cross piece of wood.
This dasher was placed inside the churn and the top tightly covered by a wooden lid

p. 9with a hole in the center for the stick. The milk had to be agitated by the up and down motion of the dasher for about 35 to 40 minutes or until small bits of butter rose to the top. The butter was gathered by the gentle sideways motion of the dasher which formed the butter into a solid mass. The butter was removed by a large spoon and placed in a bowl to be whipped to remove excess milk, and salt was added to boost the flavor. The butter was pressed into a round, wooden mold and then the handle was pushed down, placing the butter on a saucer with a design imprinted on the molded butter.

Another winter-time chore was making lye hominy. A dozen ears of white, big-grain, dry corn were shelled, the defective kernels removed, and the dried corn boiled in water and lye for 8 to 10 hours. When the grains began to swell and crack open, they were removed with a large spoon or dipper into a washtub of fresh water; when cool enough to handle, all husks were removed and the lye washed off and the mixture was cooked for 8 more hours in fresh water. If a small amount of hominy was needed, the old black iron pot used for cooking in the fireplace was large enough. If a larger pot was needed, the old washpot was suitable.

To conserve wood, the fireplace was frequently used for cooking. Items such as sweet potatoes were baked in a deep iron oven. This oven had three legs and was placed over a small pile of hot coals. The lid was placed on top and more hot coals piled on the lid. The lid could be removed with a poker to check the food. The oven was also used for baking cornbread. Hot cornbread in a bowl covered with fresh milk or buttermilk was often served as the evening meal.

Soap making usually occurred in the fall or winter after hog-killing time. The fat rendered was used for making the brownish, harsh soap used for laundry and household cleaning, as well as the "Saturday night bath." One can of lye, 6 lbs of fat, and three gallons of water were cooked in the washpot for several hours. The resulting soap rose to the top, after cooling for several days it hardened and was cut into irregular shapes to be stored on shelves to dry and cure. If lye was not available, hickory ashes could be substituted.

Finally, a parting word of advice to young descendants: hold your head high, stand tall, be proud of yourself, set a goal, and aim high. Earthy basics of deep moral values are as applicable today as in simpler, nostalgia times when grass was mowed, not smoked; when coke was a soft drink, not something to sniff. When we receive a harsh reminder of our own mortality, material things are not as important as once thought to be. More important are attributes of kindness, truthfulness, honesty, and integrity.

A popular song of World War II sums it up this way: "Accentuate the Positive, Eliminate The Negative, and Don't Mess with Mister-In-Between." Think positive, speak positive, act positive, and be an asset, not a liability, to yourself, your family, your community, and your country. Make every day count, taking advantage of all opportunities in your young years. Old age creeps upon a person and grabs from behind, leaving him with the question, "Where did the young years go"?

Before the Creek cession. The area that became Jefferson County was part of a large neutral ground between the Creek, Cherokee, Chickasaw, and Choctaw nations.

Section 21, W2SW, 80 acres, cash, patent 10 Jun 1826, patent 4869. The earliest entry in this group (patent 1826). This eighty lies directly south of the two Graham forties in Section 21. How Zacheriah Staggs connects to Rebecca Staggs Graham: Unresolved.

Section 21, SWNW, 40 acres, cash, entered before 1834, patent 14 Oct 1834, patent 8225, written "William Grimes". The earliest Graham-name patent in the township, two years before the 1836 entries. Not in our tract-book transcription because its page (118) was never scanned. That this is William (about 30 in 1834): Strongly supported, not confirmed by a second record.

Section 26, NWNE, 40.08 acres, cash, $1.25 an acre, entered 23 Jun 1836, patent 20 Sep 1839, cert. 19602. Entered four days after William's forty in Section 28. Written "Thomas Graham." Sold to John Belcher 6 Sep 1844, "Thomas Graham, his mark" (deed vol. 9 pp30 to 31). Thompson's age in 1836: about 56 to 65 (Computed from the 1830 and 1840 censuses).
Section 28, NWSE, 40.13 acres, cash, $1.25 an acre, entered 19 Jun 1836, patent 20 Sep 1839, cert. 19542. William's first dated entry, four days before Thompson's.
Section 26, SWNE, 40.08 acres, cash, entered 6 Oct 1836, patent 20 Sep 1839, cert. 20995 (patent index: 20795). The forty directly south of Thompson's.

Section 33, NWNE, 40.68 acres, bought 13 May 1839 (deed vol. 7 p251), entered 8 Oct 1836 (Gowins), patent 20 Sep 1839, in Gowins's name (written Goins), cert. 20829, written "James Goins". James Gowins (patent written "James Goins") sold this forty to Thomas Graham between his entry and his patent, so no Graham name is on the patent. The deed date is 13 May 1839 (START HERE, corrected from 1838). The younger Thomas was about 16 then, so the buyer is taken to be Thompson (Strongly supported). A "Thomas Graham" bought the same forty from Killough 19 Mar 1853; which Thomas: Unresolved.

Section 21, NWNW, 40 acres, cash, patent 10 Jul 1844, patent 23812, written "Thomas Grimes". Patented the same day as Thomas Jr's forty in Section 29, and directly north of William's 1834 forty. Which Thomas (Thompson or his grandson's generation): Unresolved.

Section 29, NESE, 40.02 acres, cash, $1.25 an acre, entered 6 May 1844, patent 10 Jul 1844, cert. 23835, written "Thomas Grimes Jr". Thomas, about 21. Entry to patent in nine weeks. Graham Cemetery is on this forty.
Section 27, SWNW, 40.10 acres, cash, entered 23 Nov 1852, patent 1 Aug 1853, cert. 27296, written "William Grimes". The tract book reads "S½ NW¼ (part)"; the patent gives SW¼ NW¼.
Section 28, NESE, 40.13 acres, cash, entered 12 Mar 1853, patent 1 Aug 1853, cert. 27637, written "William Grimes". Adjoins his 1836 forty.

Section 28, SWSE SWNE, 80.82 acres, Graduation Act, 12½¢ an acre, entered 21 Dec 1854, patent 1 Jun 1858, cert. 31399. 80.82 acres at 12.5 cents an acre, about ten dollars (Computed). Our tract-book transcription puts one forty in Section 33; the patent puts both in Section 28, which is what is drawn.

Section 29, SESE, 40.03 acres, Graduation Act, 12½¢ an acre, entered 22 Dec 1854, patent 1 Jun 1858, cert. 31397, written "William Grimes". Entered one day after Thomas's entry. Its north side touches Thomas's 1844 forty (the cemetery forty).

Section 27, NWNW, 40 acres, cash, patent 1 Jun 1858, patent 35727, written "William Grimes". In the patent index but not in our tract-book transcription, so the entry date is not known. Placed at 1856 on the year slider (Approximate).

Section 29, W2SE, 80.05 acres, Graduation Act, 12½¢ an acre, entered 11 Dec 1858, patent 2 Jul 1860, cert. 37133. The last Graham entry before the war. Its NW¼ SE¼ lies across today's Mount Olive Road from the cemetery.

Section 28, E2NW, 80.27 acres, homestead, entered Sep 1870, patent 9 Apr 1878 (tract book: 26 Jan 1876), homestead 3427 · patent 779, written "William Grimes". The family's first homestead claim, five years after the war.

Section 28, W2NE, 80.97 acres, homestead, entered 26 Apr 1871, patent 21 Nov 1889, homestead 11606 · patent 5718, written "William Grimes". This takes in the SW¼ NE¼ that Thomas entered in 1854. Why it was claimed again: Unresolved (Thomas's estate file may explain it). The patent is dated six years after William's death.

Section 28, SESE, 40.13 acres, homestead, entered 28 Mar 1877, patent 7 Oct 1889, homestead 7391 · patent 18724, written "Nancy A. Grayham". Thomas's widow, filing in her own name thirteen years after his death (January 1864). It touches William's 1853 forty.

Section 28, E2SW, 80.27 acres, homestead, entered 28 Mar 1879, patent 30 Mar 1885, homestead 7590 · patent 3598, written "Isaac J. Grayham". Nancy's son. Entered two years to the day after his mother's filing.

Section 28, W2SW, 80.27 acres, homestead, entered 20 Dec 1886, patent 21 Nov 1889, homestead 18913 · patent 5816, written "Isaac J. Grayham". An additional entry adjoining his first. It runs along the Section 29 line.

Section 32, W2SW NESW, about 120 acres, homestead, entered 13 Dec 1886, patent 23 Nov 1891, homestead 18843 · patent 9755. Drawn from the 1891 patent. Our tract-book transcription lists different forties (W½ NW¼, SE¼ NW¼); Thomas Parry patented the W½ NW¼ in 1892, so the patent is followed. Which John this is: Unresolved.

Section 32, W2SE SESE, about 120 acres, homestead, entered 22 Dec 1886, patent 19 Mar 1890, homestead 18920 · patent 6208. William and Rebecca's daughter. Entered nine days after John's entry. The tract book also lists the SE¼ SW¼; the patent does not.

Section 20, N2SE SWSE, about 120 acres, homestead, patent 21 Nov 1889, patent 5546, written "Nelley C. Grayham". Probably Nellie (Bolling) Graham, wife of Thomas's son William H. (name match). Not in our tract-book transcription; entry date not known, placed at 1886 on the year slider (Approximate).

NE¼ SE¼ Sec. 29 (Thomas Graham's 1844 forty) The dot is the GPS point on Rebecca Staggs Graham's Find a Grave memorial, about 60 yards north of the cemetery's general map pin (which lands on a driveway). Red wolf (present until early 1920s). Once lived in a variety of habitats statewide, in small groups; also took sheep, goats, pigs, and sometimes calves. Reported near extinction in Alabama in 1921 and gone by the early 1920s. Documented Outdoor Alabama, Red wolf

Bald eagle (present). Present in Alabama in William's time (General history). Killed by people, and later harmed by pesticides, in the early 1900s; killing them was not outlawed until the Bald Eagle Protection Act of 1940. General history Alabama Ornithological Society; Alabama Today

Passenger pigeon (present, then gone). Wintered across the South in huge flocks and roosts. Extinct in the wild by the early 1900s; the last known bird died at the Cincinnati Zoo, 1 Sep 1914. An Alabama or Jefferson County account is still to find. General history Then and now, section 7 (to be sourced)
Chuck-will's-widow (still here). A native summer resident that nests on the ground in open woods (General history, to be sourced). General history Then and now, section 6

A dark night sky (dark skies). No city glow before Birmingham was founded in 1871. From a dark sky the winter Milky Way runs up past Orion and the Orion Nebula is visible to the eye. General history Then and now, section 1

Sun time (sun time). Before standard time each town kept its own sun time. The railroads' time zones took effect 18 Nov 1883 (to verify). William died 28 Oct 1883, three weeks before. General history Then and now, section 2

Nine-banded armadillo (arrived 1940s). None in Alabama in William's time; first recorded in the United States in Texas in 1849. First noted in Alabama in the 1940s around Mobile County; now across most of the state except the rocky northeast. LEE GRAHAM (NMI) World War II Service & Family Research Notes 487th Bomb Group • 837th Bomb Squadron • Eighth Air Force Prepared for family preservation • October 1, 2026 Purpose of this file This is a living family-research file. It separates documented facts, strong archival leads, family oral history, and working estimates so that the stories are preserved without turning uncertainty into fact. Research status key CONFIRMED Supported by a named archival or unit-history source. STRONG LEAD Evidence is specific and credible, but an additional primary record would strengthen it. FAMILY HISTORY A recollection passed down in the family; preserved here as told, not presented as proven.

WORKING ESTIMATE A reasoned estimate with substantial uncertainty; not a historical fact. 1. What is conﬁrmed so far Lee Graham was born August 13, 1922, and died July 6, 1995. Online genealogical records place him in Adamsville, Jefferson County, Alabama. Joe has confirmed that this is his grandfather. ● Military role: Corporal, tail gunner. ● Unit: 837th Bomb Squadron, 487th Bomb Group (Heavy), U.S. Army Air Forces, Eighth Air Force. ● Base in England: Station 137, RAF Lavenham, Suffolk.

● Aircraft association: B-24H Liberator serial 42-52748, “Old Gray Gull” / “Old Grey Gull.” ● The 837th Bomb Squadron used fuselage code 4F; Old Grey Gull is identified in surviving aircraft-photo records as 4F-N while with the 487th. The strongest individual record found is the Imperial War Museums / American Air Museum “American Archive” entry for Lee Graham. Lee Graham – American Archive It identifies him as an American corporal and tail gunner, lists B-24 42-52748 Old Gray Gull, and connects him to both the 487th Bomb Group and 837th Bomb Squadron. The entry states that its sources were the National Museum of the Mighty Eighth Air Force and the 487th Bomb Group roster.
Lee Graham WWII Family Research • saved 2026-10-01

2. The unit and the aircraft The 487th Bomb Group arrived at Lavenham equipped with B-24 Liberators and began combat operations in May 1944. The group was pulled from combat on July 19, 1944, to convert to the B-17 Flying Fortress; the 837th completed the transition on August 1, 1944. 487th Bomb Group history at Lavenham Airfield 837th Bomb Squadron history That matters because Lee’s family remembered him as a B-17 gunner, while the surviving personal record ties him to a B-24. Both can be true: his squadron flew B-24s first and B-17s afterward. Old Grey Gull was B-24H-15-FO serial 42-52748.

Surviving B-24 photo-reference pages identify it as an Eighth Air Force / 487th Bomb Group / 837th Bomb Squadron aircraft, code 4F-N. The aircraft was later transferred to the 450th Bomb Group in the Fifteenth Air Force. Sources agree on the transfer but differ on the exact date of its later crash landing in Italy, so that detail remains open for verification. 3. Photographs and visual leads At least three online image-reference pages exist for Old Grey Gull.

These are photographs of the aircraft, not yet confirmed photographs of Lee himself: ● Old Grey Gull – Photo 1 ● Old Grey Gull – Photo 2 ● Old Grey Gull – Photo 3 The 487th Bomb Group Association roster is especially important because its roster pages explicitly include links to individual portraits, crew photographs, and aircraft photographs where available. 487th Bomb Group roster 4. Family oral history to preserve Story 1 – The nose gunner survived As remembered by Joe from his father: on one bombing run the crew encountered flak and enemy fire. The nose gunner was hit or his position was badly damaged, and the crew believed he had been killed.

When they returned to base, they discovered that he was still strapped in and alive even though the glass around his position was gone or shattered. Research note: This story is mechanically plausible for a B-24H. That model introduced an Emerson A-15 powered nose turret, making “nose gunner” a natural description. The later B-17G also had heavy forward armament, though its chin turret was normally controlled from the bombardier/navigator area. The specific incident has not yet been matched to a mission report or crew narrative. Story 2 – Throwing equipment overboard to make England As remembered by Joe from his father: on another return flight the aircraft was dangerously low on fuel.

The crew threw out anything that was not bolted down while crossing the English Channel in an effort to reduce weight and get home. Research note: Fuel emergencies were a real and recurring hazard for 487th Bomb Group crews. Group histories document aircraft diverting, landing with engines quitting from fuel starvation, and in at least one case a 487th B-24 being lost in the Channel after running out of fuel. None of those examples has yet been tied to Lee, so this family story remains unverified but historically plausible. Lee Graham WWII Family Research • saved 2026-10-01

5. Scale of the 487th Bomb Group’s combat Group statistic Recorded figure Combat missions 185 Credited sorties 6,021 Bomb tonnage about 14,000–14,600 tons (sources vary by accounting method) Enemy aircraft claims 22 destroyed, 6 probable, 18 damaged 487th aircrew killed 233 names commemorated at Lavenham The group-level numbers give context, but they cannot by themselves tell us exactly what Lee’s individual crew experienced. Reconstructing his mission list is the key next step. 6.

Preliminary estimate of people killed by Lee’s crew WORKING ESTIMATE  -  LOW CONFIDENCE The best current order-of-magnitude estimate is that the crew may have caused roughly single-digit to low-teen deaths over a full combat tour, mostly through bombing rather than defensive gunfire. A much wider range  -  from zero to several dozen  -  remains plausible. This is not a historical finding; it is a statistical placeholder until Lee’s actual missions and targets are identified. Defensive guns: No source found so far credits Lee personally with shooting down an enemy aircraft. The entire 487th Bomb Group claimed 22 enemy aircraft destroyed across 6,021 credited sorties.

Until a combat claim or mission report names Lee or his crew, his confirmed aerial-kill count should be treated as zero confirmed, not necessarily zero actual. Bombing casualties: Attributing casualties to a single bomber is inherently difficult. Aircraft usually bombed in formation, many targets were military or transportation targets, and casualty totals were often recorded at the raid or city level rather than by individual airplane. The U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey estimated at least 305,000 people killed by Allied bombing in Germany, but applying that broad figure directly to one aircraft would create false precision. The mission-by-mission route is far more defensible. 7.

Best next research steps ● Reconstruct Lee Graham’s exact mission dates, aircraft assignments, and crew positions from 487th Bomb Group loading lists, special orders, morning reports, and mission records. ● Identify the pilot/crew under whom Lee normally flew. Crew photographs and narratives are often indexed under the pilot rather than the gunner. ● Search the 487th photo archive and National Museum of the Mighty Eighth Air Force holdings for Lee Graham, Old Grey Gull, serial 42-52748, and the eventual pilot/crew name. ● Compare the two family stories against mission reports for battle damage, wounded crew, emergency landings, fuel shortages, and jettisoned equipment.
● Once the mission list is known, examine target-specific after-action reports and local casualty records before revising the casualty estimate. Lee Graham WWII Family Research • saved 2026-10-01

I MOUN T O L I V E · J E F F E R SON COUN T Y · A L A B AMA What happened to Thomas Graham About 1823 to January 1864 n the autumn of 1863 a farmer named Thomas Graham was living in the woods above Mount Olive, in the north end of Jefferson County, Alabama. He had a wife and eight children in a house he could not go to. He was about forty years old. He was hiding from the Confederate army. T H E G R O U N D H E C A M E F R O M His people had been in that county since it was made. His grandfather Thompson came out of South Carolina and bought eighty acres on Village Creek in 1825, land that is now the Woodlawn neighbourhood of Birmingham, back when Birmingham did not exist.

He sold it two years later and moved north to the hills around Mount Olive. In June 1836 Thompson and his son William walked into the federal land office at Tuscaloosa four days apart and each paid fifty dollars and ten cents for forty acres. Four months later Ezekiel Staggs bought the forty directly adjoining Thompson's, and two days after that a neighbour named James Goins bought the forty that he would sell on to the family eighteen months later. These were not strangers.

The 1830 census of Jefferson County lists the Grahams, the Staggses, the Jameses and the Belchers within a few lines of each other, which means within a few farms, and over the next three generations those four families married into one another over and over. Thomas was born into that in about 1823. In 1845 he married Nancy Ann James, whose father had been living down the road since before either of them could remember. They had eight children. In December 1854 he bought eighty acres of his own for ten dollars and eleven cents, and in December 1858 he bought eighty more. He was a man with 1

land, a wife, and a house full of children, and he was about thirty-eight years old when the war started. H E S A I D H E W O U L D N O T G O Alabama left the Union in January 1861, but the hill counties of the north were never much persuaded. There were few large farms up there and almost no enslaved people, and a great many men could not see what the quarrel had to do with them. Thomas was one of them. His wife said so under oath, eleven years later: I was in favor of the union from the commencement of the war to the end of the war.

My feelings was all the time in favor of the union cause and desired the union army to succeed and put down the rebellion, and I expressed my sentiments publicly to both sides in that way. I told my friends and relatives not to go into the rebel army, but to keep out of it. I told my husband not to go into the rebel army, and he always told me that he would not until he was conscripted. Nancy Ann Graham, sworn at Elyton, 26 July 1872 In April 1862 the Confederacy passed the first conscription act in American history. Men of military age were no longer asked. Thomas kept his word in the only way left to him. He went into the woods. LY I N G O U T There was a phrase for it in those hills.

Men who would not serve were said to be lying out, and there were enough of them that the Confederate cavalry made a regular business of hunting them. The pressure was not applied to the man. It was applied to his family.

I heard that while the Claimants husband was lying out in the woods to keep from being Conscripted and forced into the rebel army, that if the Claimants husband did not come in and give up and go to the rebel army that they would go to the Claimants house and remain till they the Cavalry eat up everything that she had, and under these threats and with the promise that if he would come in that they would give him a furlough so that he could prepare himself to go to the rebel army, the husband of the claimant came in and was put in jail as stated. The claimant was opposed to her husband doing this. I know this of my own knowledge. Julian Nail, sworn at Elyton, 1872 2

Read that twice. They told him that if he did not come in, they would sit in his house and eat his family's food until it was gone. And they told him that if he did come in, they would give him a furlough so he could get his affairs in order. He came in. There was no furlough. They put him in the jail at Elyton. The man who swore to that had reason to know. Julian Nail had hidden in those same woods, had been fed by Nancy while he was hiding, and later made his way to Union lines and served twelve months in Company D of the First Alabama Cavalry, United States Army. He had also married Nancy's sister. T H E J A I L AT E LY TO N Nancy went to him. So did his father.

I saw my son Thomas Graham nearly every day from the time that the war commenced up to the time that he was arrested and sent off to the Army. I saw him one time after he was arrested, he was then in jail at Elyton. I heard that he had been arrested by the conscript officers and put in jail and I went with his wife the claimant to Elyton to see him and when we got to Elyton we found him in jail and he told us that he had been arrested by the conscript officers and put in jail and that he would be sent off to the Army in a few days. I never saw him after that time. William Graham, aged 68, the father of the deceased, sworn 1873 Nancy said he had not changed his mind.

He told her, in the jail, that he was opposed to the war and would not fight for the rebel cause. He was not allowed to go home. They sent him off a few days later. TA L L A D E G A , A N D T H E N C H AT TA N O O G A He went first to the conscript camp at Talladega, about seventy miles southeast, where Alabama gathered the men it had taken. From there he was forwarded to the army at Chattanooga. He did not last. The finding of fact, written in Washington by the three Commissioners of Claims who later reviewed his widow's case, puts it in one sentence: 3

Her husband was arrested by the Confederates in the fall of '63 & forced to go to the Conscript Camp at Talladega & then to Chattanooga where he died the day after his arrival in Jany '64. Commissioners of Claims, on claim no. 7100 The day after he arrived. He had been taken out of his house, held in a county jail, marched seventy miles to a camp, and sent on to an army he had spent two years refusing to join, and then he was dead. Whether it was disease, which killed far more men than bullets did, or something else, no record says. He was about forty. His youngest child was eighteen months old. The family has always said he was buried in a military cemetery at Chattanooga.

That may well be true, and it is the one part of this account that no document confirms. W H AT N A N C Y D I D She was about thirty-eight, with eight children and a farm. In the last days of March 1865, with the war nearly over, Union cavalry under General James Wilson rode through Jefferson County on their way to Selma and took what was left: a mare, a mule, four hundred bushels of corn, three hundred pounds of bacon, a thousand pounds of fodder, eleven bushels of oats, and a saddle and bridle. They were the army her husband had refused to fight, and they cleaned out her barn.

Six years later Congress created a commission to pay loyal southerners for property the Union army had taken, and Nancy filed. To be paid she had to prove she had been for the Union the whole time, which meant proving in sworn detail that her husband had been dragged into the Confederate army rather than walking into it. That is the only reason any of this was ever written down. She could not bring her witnesses to Washington. The file records why, in the plainest words in it: she was too poor to procure the attendance of said witnesses. So the testimony was taken at Elyton instead, and the neighbours came and swore to what they had seen.

The Commissioners allowed her five hundred and fifty-five dollars and fifty cents. They thought she had overstated the corn and the bacon, judged the mare not worth more than a hundred dollars at eleven years old, and refused the saddle. It was still more than four 4

times the hundred and twenty-five dollars at which her husband's entire estate had been valued. She never remarried. In 1877 she filed a homestead claim on forty acres in her own name, and two years later her son Isaac filed on the eighty beside hers. She lived until 1911 and is buried at Graham Cemetery, forty-seven years a widow. T H E C H I L D R E N In 1873 she listed them for the commissioner, by name and age, and said they were all living and all at home with her: William, twenty-seven. Thomas, twenty-five. Sarah, twenty-three. John, twenty-one. Isaac, nineteen. Rebecca, seventeen. Nancy, fifteen. And last, aged ten, a boy the clerk wrote down as Minnie. That was I. N.

Graham, known in the family all his life as Nin. He was about two years old when they took his father, and too young to remember him. He grew up, married Martha Melissa Brooks, and had seven children of his own, and the line that reaches the Grahams of Mount Olive today runs straight through that ten-year-old boy at the bottom of his mother's list. She also told the commissioner something easy to read past. Her two eldest sons, William and Thomas, had been seventeen and fifteen when their father was taken, and she said they never went into the rebel army, that they stayed at home all the time and said they never intended to fight against the United States government.

After what had been done to her husband, she kept her boys out of it. W H Y N O B O D Y K N E W The family history that has been passed around for forty years gives him one line. It says he died in 1864 in the Civil War and was buried at Chattanooga, and leaves you to assume he went like everyone else went. He did not. He hid in the woods until they starved his family out, he was lied to about a furlough, he was jailed in his own county, and he was sent to his death in an army he had told his wife and his father and a jailhouse full of men that he would not fight for.
All of it was written down in 1872 and 1873, in sworn testimony, in a federal file that sat unread for a hundred and fifty years. 5

W H E R E T H I S C O M E S F R O M Every quotation in this account is from sworn testimony in the Southern Claims Commission file of Nancy Ann Graham, claim number 7100, Jefferson County, Alabama. The file runs to sixty-two pages and is held by the National Archives, Microfilm Publication M2062, Record Group 217. The depositions were taken at Elyton, the county seat before Birmingham, by Special Commissioner John Brown in July 1872 and again in 1873. Nancy Ann Graham, the widow, deposed 26 July 1872 and again in 1873. She signed with her mark. Julian Nail, farmer, aged about forty, of Jefferson County.

Served twelve months in Company D, First Alabama Cavalry, United States Army, under Colonel Spencer; honourably discharged at Huntsville. Married Nancy's sister. J. W. Rowe, farmer, who had himself been conscripted, sent to Talladega, and escaped to the woods before reaching Union service. William Graham, aged sixty-eight, the father of the deceased. He signed with his mark. The Commissioners of Claims, Asa Owen Aldis, James B. Howell and Orange Ferriss, whose written finding of fact appears on the claim summary sheet. The estate record is a certified transcript made by Judge John C. Morrow of the Jefferson County Probate Court on 19 November 1873, bound into the same file.

It records that William Graham was appointed administrator of his son's estate on 26 February 1866, that the estate was worth about one hundred and twenty-five dollars, and that the final settlement was made on 15 January 1869. The eight heirs are listed by name. Other details come from the 1830 and 1850 federal censuses of Jefferson County, from federal land patents and the Tuscaloosa land office tract books for Township 15 South, Range 3 West, and from the compiled Graham family history, pages 111 to 126. One honest caution. The family has always said Thomas was buried in a military cemetery at Chattanooga, and the sworn testimony says he died there in January 1864.

By that month Chattanooga was held by Union forces and the Confederate army had withdrawn into Georgia, which leaves a question nobody has yet answered about exactly where he died and where he lies. The burial is the single part of this story that rests on family memory alone. Everything else in these pages is in a document somebody swore to. 6
